title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 32
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Somewhere to Be Ill
passages.text:
A. For most of history the hospital was not a place where people went to be cured. It was a place of shelter for travellers, the destitute and the dying, run by religious orders, and its function was care in the sense of tending rather than treatment. Anyone with a home and money was treated in it, by a physician who came to them, and the hospital was where you went when you had neither.

B. That inheritance shaped the buildings long after their purpose changed. Large open wards, communal facilities and an institutional character followed from an origin in shelter rather than in medicine, and they persisted because they were cheap to staff and because nobody with a choice was using them. The design served the institution's economics and not the patient's recovery, and the distinction was not one anyone was required to make.

C. Infection is what forced the change and it was resisted at every step. Hospitals of the period were more dangerous than homes for anyone undergoing a procedure, a fact visible in outcome records before it was explicable, and the practices that reduced it — separating cases, washing hands, sterilising instruments — were adopted slowly because they implied that those attending patients had been carrying the harm. Explanations that assign blame to the professional are adopted more slowly than those that do not.

D. Specialisation reorganised the hospital around the equipment. Once diagnosis and treatment depended on machines too expensive to duplicate, care concentrated where the machines were, and the hospital became a building organised around apparatus rather than around patients. This concentration produced real gains, since volume improves outcomes for complex procedures, and produced the familiar experience of being moved between departments each of which sees a part.

E. The measurement of hospital performance has proved harder than its advocates expected. Outcomes depend heavily on which patients arrive, so an institution taking the most difficult cases will look worse than one that does not, and adjustment for this is imperfect and gameable. Published comparisons have measurably changed behaviour, including the avoidance of high-risk patients, which is an improvement in the statistic and not in the care.

F. The direction of change now is away from the building altogether. Procedures once requiring days of admission are done in a morning; monitoring that required a bed is done at home; and the most expensive resource in the system is the overnight stay that much of the estate was built to provide. A century of institutional investment is being partly reversed, which is a difficult thing for organisations whose identity is a place.

passages.title: The Weight on the Slope
passages.text:
Snow is not a substance but a record. Each fall arrives with a structure determined by the temperature and humidity that formed it, and once on the ground it continues to change — crystals shrink, bond and recrystallise — so a snowpack is a stack of layers of differing strength laid down over a season. Avalanches are a problem of what lies between those layers rather than of snow itself.

The dangerous arrangement is a strong layer resting on a weak one. A cohesive slab of wind-packed or settled snow can sit on a buried layer of loose faceted crystals or surface hoar, and the slab holds together well enough to distribute a load across a wide area. When the weak layer fails at any point, the failure can propagate beneath the slab, and a large area releases at once as a single unit — which is why fatal avalanches are usually slab releases and why they can be triggered from below or beside the slope that slides.

Cold, clear weather is what creates the weak layers, which is the least intuitive part of the subject. A thin snowpack under a cold clear sky loses heat rapidly at the surface, producing a steep temperature gradient through the snow, and that gradient drives the growth of large angular crystals that bond poorly. A long settled cold spell therefore builds instability into the pack, and the avalanche it enables may occur weeks later during the next substantial snowfall.

Human triggering accounts for the great majority of avalanche deaths, and the pattern of it is consistent. Victims are typically experienced rather than ignorant, the slope has typically been skied before, and the decision to proceed is typically made after observing that others have done so safely. Familiarity, prior success and the presence of a group all reduce the perceived risk without changing the physical situation at all.

Forecasting has become good at the regional scale and cannot become good at the scale that matters. A bulletin can state that conditions across an area are dangerous, because that follows from weather and snowpack observation; whether a particular slope will release under a particular person cannot be determined without knowing the weak layer's condition at that point, which is not observable from the surface. The gap between regional forecast and individual slope is permanent.

What reduces deaths is therefore procedural rather than predictive. Travelling one at a time on suspect slopes, carrying and practising with rescue equipment, choosing lower-angle terrain when the bulletin is unfavourable, and treating a group's willingness as a hazard rather than a reassurance are all measures that work by lowering exposure. None requires knowing what the slope will do, which is the point.

passages.title: Who Gains from the Ground
passages.text:
Public subsidy for sports stadiums is among the most studied questions in applied economics, and among the few where the academic literature is close to unanimous while public policy continues in the opposite direction. Study after study, across countries and decades and methods, finds that the local economic benefits claimed for such projects do not appear in the data. The disagreement is not really about evidence.

The claimed mechanism is straightforward and the flaw in it is equally so. A stadium is said to bring spending into an area, creating employment and tax revenue. Most of that spending, however, is not new but relocated: households have a budget for entertainment, and money spent at a match is largely money not spent at cinemas, restaurants and other venues in the same region. Substitution consumes most of the apparent gain before anything is counted.

The employment created has a shape that aggregate figures hide. Stadium jobs are disproportionately part-time, seasonal and low-paid, concentrated on a few dozen days a year, and the construction employment is temporary by definition. Comparing the number of jobs to the subsidy per job produces figures that would be rejected immediately in any other category of public spending, and the comparison is rarely made in the documents that authorise the spending.

Where value genuinely appears, it is not the value being claimed. Residents often report attachment to a team and pleasure in its presence that is real, measurable by survey methods, and unconnected to economic activity — the benefit is consumption, not investment. That is a legitimate reason for public support, argued honestly it would be a much weaker case for the sums involved, and it is almost never the argument made.

The bargaining position explains the persistence better than the economics do. A team can credibly threaten to move, cities compete against one another to retain or attract one, and the resulting auction transfers public money to private owners regardless of what any study concludes. Individual cities behave rationally within a structure that produces a collectively poor outcome, which is why the few effective remedies have involved coordination between cities rather than better analysis within them.

The pattern generalises beyond sport, which is the reason the case is worth understanding. Any mobile enterprise able to threaten relocation can extract subsidy from competing jurisdictions, the promised benefits are typically evaluated by consultants engaged by the beneficiary, and the evaluation arrives before the decision while the outcome arrives long after anyone is accountable for it. Stadiums are simply the version of this with the best-documented literature.
